content.overview: BNS s. 51 — Liability of abettor when one act abetted and different act done.
content.study:
Introduction and meaning
Liability of abettor when one act abetted and different act done. BNS restatement of IPC 111. Elements are substantially the same; cite the BNS number for offences on or after 1 July 2024. BNS restatement of IPC 111. Cite the BNS number for facts on or after 1 July 2024.
In student language: BNS s. 51 is the rule on “Liability of abettor when one act abetted and different act done”. The section provides that when an act is abetted and a different act is done, the abettor is liable for the act done, in the same manner and to the same extent as if he had directly abetted it:. Do not stop at the heading. An examiner awards marks for the ingredients, the explanations and the illustrations, not for writing the title alone.

Why this is asked
Criminal law arguments turn on statutory ingredients. BNS s. 51 exists so that “Liability of abettor when one act abetted and different act done” has a closed legal test in Chapter IV — Of Abetment, Criminal Conspiracy and Attempt. An authoritative analysis defines the concept, lists every ingredient, walks the statutory illustrations, states exceptions, and applies the test methodically to facts.
Chapter setting: The inchoate trio. Abetment now covers extra-territorial aid; conspiracy and attempt sit next to it.

The provision in detail
51. When an act is abetted and a different act is done, the abettor is liable for the act done, in the same manner and to the same extent as if he had directly abetted it:

Essential ingredients
1. When an act is abetted and a different act is done, the abettor is liable for the act done, in the same manner and to the same extent as if he had directly abetted it:

Statutory illustrations
Illustration (a). A instigates a child to put poison into the food of Z, and gives him poison for that purpose. The child, in consequence of the instigation, by mistake puts the poison into the food of Y, which is by the side of that of Z. Here, if the child was acting under the influence of A’s instigation, and the act done was under the circumstances a probable consequence of the abetment, A is liable in the same manner and to the same extent as if he had instigated the child to put the poison into the food of Y

Exam use: quote illustration (a), then write which ingredient of BNS s. 51 it proves. Copying the illustration without that mapping sentence does not score.

Illustration (b). A instigates B to burn Z’s house, B sets fire to the house and at the same time commits theft of property there. A, though guilty of abetting the burning of the house, is not guilty of abetting the theft; for the theft was a distinct act, and not a probable consequence of the burning

Exam use: quote illustration (b), then write which ingredient of BNS s. 51 it proves. Copying the illustration without that mapping sentence does not score.

Illustration (c). A instigates B and C to break into an inhabited house at midnight for the purpose of robbery, and provides them with arms for that purpose. B and C break into the house, and being resisted by Z, one of the inmates, murder Z. Here, if that murder was the probable consequence of the abetment, A is liable to the punishment provided for murder

Exam use: quote illustration (c), then write which ingredient of BNS s. 51 it proves. Copying the illustration without that mapping sentence does not score.

Exceptions, limitations and provisos
Provided that the act done was a probable consequence of the abetment, and was committed under the influence of the instigation, or with the aid or in pursuance of the conspiracy which constituted the abetment

learningObjectives: Master the 'probable consequence' doctrine under BNS s. 51.
Analyze the twin requirements: different act was a probable consequence, and committed under influence of abetment.
Differentiate foreseeable escalation from totally unexpected, independent crimes.
enhancement.definition: BNS s. 51 provides that when an act is abetted and a different act is done, the abettor is liable for the act done, in the same manner and to the same extent as if he had directly abetted it: Provided the act done was a probable consequence of the abetment, and was committed under the influence of the instigation, or with the aid or in pursuance of the conspiracy which constituted the abetment.
enhancement.legalPrinciple: An abettor who unleashes an unlawful force is constructively liable for an unintended, different crime committed by the perpetrator, provided that different crime was a natural and probable consequence of the abetment and occurred under its continuous influence.
statutoryFramework: Chapter IV — Of Abetment, Criminal Conspiracy and Attempt, BNS s. 51 (corresponding to IPC s. 111).
Scenario: Act A is abetted, but the perpetrator commits Act B.
Liability rule: Abettor is liable for Act B as if directly abetted.
Mandatory Proviso Limb 1: Act B must be a 'probable consequence' of the abetment.
Mandatory Proviso Limb 2: Act B must be committed 'under the influence of the instigation' or in pursuance of the conspiracy/aid.
essentialIngredients: The accused abetted a particular act.
A different act was committed by the person abetted.
The act done was a probable consequence of the original abetment (objectively foreseeable).
The act done was committed under the influence of the instigation or in pursuance of the conspiracy.
enhancement.detailedExplanation: Section 51 codifies the common law doctrine of collateral or probable consequences. An abettor cannot set a dangerous criminal enterprise into motion and then wash his hands of foreseeable escalations. 'Probable consequence' means an outcome which a reasonable person in the abettor's position would contemplate as likely to occur in the ordinary course of executing the abetted crime. If A instigates B to commit armed robbery at a bank, and B shoots a security guard who raises an alarm, shooting the guard is a probable consequence; A is liable for the murder. But if B, after robbing the bank, stops by a jewelry shop five miles away and commits rape, that is an independent frolic, not a probable consequence.
examples: Teaching example (Probable consequence of housebreaking): A instigates B to break into a family dwelling at midnight and steal silver. B breaks in; the owner wakes up and struggles; B stabs the owner with a dagger carried for the burglary. Stabbing the waking owner is a probable consequence of midnight housebreaking; A is liable under s. 51 for the stabbing.

Teaching example (Independent crime / Not a probable consequence): A instigates B to burn down an empty barn in a field. B goes to the barn, but instead goes to the owner's house and steals a car. Stealing a car is not a probable consequence of barn arson; A is not liable for car theft.
distinctions: Probable consequence (s. 51) vs Same intention: Section 51 creates constructive liability even without shared intention, grounded purely on objective foreseeability.
Section 51 vs Section 52: Section 51 establishes liability for the different act; Section 52 governs whether punishment is cumulative for both the abetted act and the different act.
problemApplication: Issue: Whether an abettor who incited an accomplice to snatch a handbag in a deserted alley is liable when the accomplice stabbed the resisting victim with a hidden switchblade.
Rule: Under BNS s. 51, an abettor is liable for a different act done if it was a probable consequence committed under the influence of the abetment.
Application: Robbery on the street with physical confrontation carries the foreseeable risk of armed resistance and violent injury. The stabbing occurred in direct execution of the robbery.
Conclusion: The stabbing was a probable consequence; the abettor is liable under s. 51.

Give the housebreaking escalating into violence illustration.

keyTakeaways: Abettor is liable for a different act if it was a probable consequence.
Must be committed under the continuing influence of the abetment.
Does not extend to wholly independent, unforeseeable crimes.
